title: What an Unfilled Classroom Costs a School District
metaTitle: Cost of a Teacher Vacancy: Calculator for School Districts
description: Put a dollar figure on an open teaching or special education seat: substitute pay, coverage, IEP minutes owed and replacement cost, with a calculator.
answer: The cost of a teacher vacancy lands in 6 places: substitute pay, coverage pay for teachers, administrator hours, lost instruction, compensatory services for missed IEP minutes, and replacing the teacher. Replacement alone runs $11,860 to $24,930 per teacher by district size, the Learning Policy Institute's 2024 estimate. The calculator below totals your own seat by the week.
keyTakeaways: Replacing 1 teacher costs $11,860 in a district under 10,000 students and $24,930 in a district over 50,000, by the Learning Policy Institute's 2024 estimate.

bodyHtml:
What is the cost of a teacher vacancy, including a special education seat?

Start with $490 a week for a substitute at $98 a day, then add $11,860 to $24,930 to replace the teacher. Those are the 2 lines with a national figure, and both are sourced below. The other 4 depend on your contract and your caseload: coverage pay, administrator hours, lost instruction and compensatory services for missed IEP minutes.

In October 2024, 35% of public schools had at least 1 teaching vacancy, and special education positions averaged 5% vacant (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, December 12, 2024 release). Before the 2024-25 school year started, public schools had filled 77% of their special education vacancies with fully certified teachers. The other 23% started the year without one (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, October 17, 2024 release).

Cost lineWhat it isWhat the sources say
Substitute coverageDaily pay for every school day the seat is open$98 to $148 a day on average across 124 large districts (NCTQ, 2019). $20.03 an hour at the national median (BLS, May 2025).
Teachers covering classesExtra pay when your own teachers give up a planning periodNearly three-quarters of public schools frequently rely on administrators and teachers on free periods to cover classes (NCES, May 2022).
Administrator hoursPosting, screening, interviewing, arranging daily coverageMedian pay for a school principal is $105,870 a year (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, school principals, May 2025).
Lost instructionSchool days students spend without a certified teacher in the seat29% of school leaders with a vacancy said class sizes went up because of it (NCES, October 2024).
Compensatory servicesIEP minutes not delivered, which the district can be ordered to make up34 CFR 300.151(b)(1) names compensatory services as a remedy.
Replacing the teacherSeparation, recruiting, hiring and training$11,860 in a district under 10,000 students, $16,450 at 10,000 to 50,000, $24,930 over 50,000 (Learning Policy Institute, 2024).

Substitute pay and coverage pay

The substitute is the cost you already see. Across 124 large districts, daily substitute pay averaged $98 to $148 (source: National Council on Teacher Quality, substitute teacher pools, 2019). The national median wage for short-term substitutes was $20.03 an hour in May 2025 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025 data tables). At $98 a day, 8 weeks of coverage is $3,920 for 1 room.

When no substitute comes, your own people cover. Nearly three-quarters of public schools told NCES they frequently rely on administrators, non-teaching staff and teachers on their free periods to cover classes (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, May 2022 collection). If your contract pays teachers for a lost planning period, that is a second payroll cost for the same seat. Planned leaves are covered in the true cost of a long-term substitute.

Lost instruction

A covered room is not a taught room. In schools with a vacancy, 29% of leaders said class sizes increased because of it, and 42% said teachers were pulled into tasks outside their intended duties (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, December 12, 2024 release). The Learning Policy Institute sums up the research in 1 line: high teacher turnover undermines student achievement (source: Learning Policy Institute, 2024 turnover calculator).

IEP minutes and compensatory services

For a special education seat, the largest cost is the one with no invoice yet. Federal rule requires that special education and related services "are made available to the child in accordance with the child's IEP" (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.323(c)(2)). A vacancy does not pause that duty. In October 2026, the Connecticut State Department of Education credited a district for posting a vacant speech-language position promptly and contracting with outside agencies. It held that the district "is still required to provide all special education and related services" in the student's IEP, and ordered compensatory education (source: Connecticut State Department of Education, complaint 27-0136).

The remedy is written into the regulation. When a state finds a failure to provide appropriate services, it must address it with corrective action "such as compensatory services or monetary reimbursement" (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.151(b)(1)). In January 2024, the Colorado Department of Education found that 1 vacant special education teacher position left 25 students without specialized instruction from February 17 to the end of the school year. It ruled the gap a denial of a free appropriate public education (FAPE) and ordered compensatory education. The same decision records that district's own practice: when a speech-language position stays open more than 2 weeks, the affected students are identified as needing compensatory education (source: Colorado Department of Education, State-Level Complaint 2023:570).

Replacing the teacher

Then you pay to hire. The Learning Policy Institute's 2024 estimate for replacing 1 teacher is $11,860 in a district under 10,000 students, $16,450 in a district of 10,000 to 50,000 and $24,930 in a district over 50,000. The figure covers separation, recruiting, hiring and training: job advertising, interviews, background and credentialing checks, mentoring and onboarding. None of the lost learning is counted in it (source: Learning Policy Institute, 2024 technical supplement).

Should you wait for a direct hire or cover the seat with a contract professional now?

Cover the seat now and keep recruiting. A contract professional stops the costs that grow by the week, and with temp-to-perm the same person can become your permanent hire.

The NCES figures in the table are from the start of the 2024-25 school year (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, October 17, 2024 release). How agency pricing works is laid out in how much a teacher staffing agency costs and in our 2026 district cost comparison. This page supplies the number on the other side of that comparison: the empty seat.

When should a district use contract staffing instead of waiting for a direct hire?

Use contract staffing when the seat carries IEP minutes, when the vacancy is past 2 weeks, or when the posting has not produced a certified candidate. In each case the cost of waiting grows every week.

  • The seat is a special education teacher. Federal rule requires each public school special education teacher to hold full state certification that has not been "waived on an emergency, temporary, or provisional basis" (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.156(c)(1)). A day-to-day substitute holds the room. A certified contract teacher delivers the IEP.
  • The seat is a related service. The same section sets the same bar for related services personnel. Wisconsin's Department of Public Instruction found a district in error for 15 speech sessions missed to provider absences, and sent the IEP team back within 20 days to decide on compensatory services (source: Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction, IDEA complaint decision 25-116).
  • The vacancy is past 2 weeks. That is the point at which the Colorado district above starts identifying students on a speech-language caseload for compensatory education.
  • The seat opened mid-year. There is no summer to recruit in. The Colorado seat emptied on February 17 and stayed empty through the last day of school.
  • The posting has drawn no certified applicant. 64% of public schools named a lack of qualified candidates as a challenge in filling teaching vacancies for 2024-25 (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, October 17, 2024 release).

Contracting is a step a state has credited. Federal rule has every state require its districts to "take measurable steps to recruit, hire, train, and retain" special education teachers who meet that certification standard (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.156(d)). Connecticut's finding listed contracting with outside agencies among the efforts that earned the district limited corrective action. Role detail is on our special education staffing and substitute teacher staffing pages.

How does temp-to-perm protect a district's budget?

Temp-to-perm lets you watch a professional work in your building before you commit to a permanent hire. With FocusedEDU the move to permanent costs nothing: no conversion fee and no buyout. Your budget is protected twice. You do not pay to convert, and you do not pay to replace a hire who only looked right on paper.

The second protection is the larger one. A teacher who leaves costs $11,860 to $24,930 to replace. In the districts that reported a breakdown, training was 55% to 87% of that cost, money that does not pay back in full when the teacher leaves within a few years (source: Learning Policy Institute, 2024 technical supplement and turnover calculator). A marking period on the real caseload, in the real classroom, is how you avoid paying that figure twice for the same seat.

FocusedEDU's terms, as they stand: every placement is temp-to-perm at no cost. Evaluate a special education teacher in your building for as long as you need.

Elias Pappas, CEO of Odyssey Charter School, put it this way in his signed letter: "Their innovative temp-to-perm clause has allowed us to assess the suitability of referred professionals before making permanent hiring decisions, all at no cost to the school." The full letter is on our references page, and the model is explained in temp-to-perm: the lowest-risk way to hire for your classroom.

How do you put a number on your own open seat?

Add up what the seat costs each week, including what it costs to make up missed IEP minutes, multiply by the weeks it stays open, and keep the minutes owed as their own count. The calculator at the top of this page does it in under a minute. The arithmetic is short enough to do on paper.

  1. Substitute coverage per week. Your daily substitute cost times 5 school days.
  2. Class coverage per week. The hours your own teachers cover, times your contract's coverage rate.
  3. Administrator time per week. The hours a principal or HR lead spends on posting, screening, interviewing and arranging coverage, times that person's hourly cost.
  4. IEP minutes per week. The students on the caseload times the IEP minutes each one is missing. Divide by 60 and multiply by what a make-up hour costs you.
  5. Cost per week and total. Add lines 1 through 4, then multiply by weeks open.
  6. Minutes owed. IEP minutes per week times weeks open.
  7. Student-days. Students times 5 times weeks open: the school days students spent without a certified teacher in the seat.

The calculator starts with a sourced figure where a national one exists: $98 a day for a substitute, the low end of the NCTQ average from 2019, so enter your current daily rate if it is higher, and the BLS median hourly wage for a make-up hour of speech-language pathology ($47.05) or occupational therapy ($48.24) (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, speech-language pathologists and occupational therapists, May 2025). For special education teachers BLS publishes annual pay only, a median of $67,170 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, special education teachers), so that hourly input starts at 0. So do your coverage rate and your administrator cost. The caseload starts at 25 students, the number in the Colorado decision. Replace each one with your own.

Here is the arithmetic with figures from the sources above. Substitute coverage for 8 weeks is $98 times 5 times 8, or $3,920. A caseload of 25 students, the number in the Colorado decision, each missing 60 minutes a week for 8 weeks is 12,000 minutes. That is 200 hours of specialized instruction for an IEP team to account for, and 1,000 student-days without a certified teacher.

Three notes on reading your result.

  • The salary you are not paying does not cancel the total. Substitute pay and coverage pay are new spending. Compensatory minutes follow the student until they are delivered. The replacement cost arrives the day you hire.
  • The minutes are counted minute for minute. The IEP team or the state sets the actual award. Colorado's decision says it is meant to restore the student to where they would have been and need not be an hour-for-hour calculation.
  • Keep the replacement cost beside the total. The Learning Policy Institute's $11,860 to $24,930 already includes recruiting time and, in some of its underlying studies, substitutes for mid-year departures.

There is no agency price in the calculator. It measures the empty seat.

faqs.q: What is the cost of teacher turnover for a school district?
faqs.a: The Learning Policy Institute's 2024 estimate is $11,860 per teacher in a district under 10,000 students, $16,450 in a district of 10,000 to 50,000 students and $24,930 in a district over 50,000. The figure covers separation, recruiting, hiring and training. It does not count missed IEP minutes or lost learning, so those costs sit on top of it.

faqs.q: Does a staffing shortage excuse a district from delivering IEP services?
faqs.a: No. 34 CFR 300.323(c)(2) requires that special education and related services are made available in accordance with the child's IEP, and it has no vacancy exception. In October 2026 the Connecticut State Department of Education found a district in violation even though it had posted the speech-language vacancy promptly and contracted with outside agencies. The state ordered compensatory education for the missed services.

faqs.q: What are compensatory services, and how are they calculated?
faqs.a: Compensatory services make up for special education or related services a student should have received. 34 CFR 300.151(b)(1) names them as a corrective action when a state finds a failure to provide appropriate services. The amount is set case by case. A 2024 Colorado Department of Education decision describes the goal as restoring the student to the position they would have been in, and says the award need not be an hour-for-hour calculation.

faqs.q: Can a substitute teacher cover a special education vacancy?
faqs.a: A substitute can supervise the room. Delivering the IEP is a different standard. Under 34 CFR 300.156(c), a public school special education teacher must hold full state special education certification, including through an approved alternate route, that has not been waived on an emergency, temporary, or provisional basis. BLS defines a short-term substitute as a temporary replacement who typically uses the regular teacher's lesson plan. A certified contract special education teacher meets the federal standard.

faqs.q: How hard is it to fill a special education teaching vacancy?
faqs.a: Hard. NCES Commissioner Peggy Carr said special education positions "remain the most difficult to fill." Before the 2024-25 school year, 74% of elementary and middle schools with a special education vacancy reported difficulty filling it with a fully certified teacher, and public schools filled 77% of special education vacancies with fully certified teachers before the first day. In October 2024, special education positions averaged 5% vacant.

faqs.q: What does temp-to-perm cost with FocusedEDU?
faqs.a: Nothing extra. Every FocusedEDU placement is temp-to-perm at no cost. You evaluate the professional in your building first, and if you hire them permanently there is no conversion fee and no buyout. Elias Pappas, CEO of Odyssey Charter School, wrote that the clause let the school assess referred professionals before making permanent hiring decisions, all at no cost to the school.

faqs.a: Run the calculator on this page, then send the result with the role and your state through the staffing request form. FocusedEDU replies with the rate range for that role in your state.
